## Chase and Physical Suspense

### Name the Pressure Before the Device

**Also called:** the tension selector, pressure before device, what is actually squeezing this scene
**What it is:** The card at the head of the `tens.` shelf. It does not describe a feeling. It asks the three questions the shelf's own pair graph asks over and over — **what is the character up against, who is ahead of whom, and how many seconds do you have** — and hands back a named shortlist for each answer. The axes were not invented: they were read off the ninety-three `Yields to:` conditions these hundred and four cards carry, and the conditions that repeated became the questions. Every card cited here is cited by id.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This card never reaches the page. It exists so that the device that does reach the page was chosen against the danger, the audience's position and the running time, rather than reached for because it is the one everybody remembers.
**Used for and where it works best:** Answer the three questions **in order and out loud, in one sentence each, before you open the shelf**. Question one eliminates between a sixth and two-fifths of the shelf; questions two and three leave a shortlist usually between three and twelve. If you cannot answer question one — *what is the character up against* — you do not have a tension problem, you have a story problem, and no card here will supply the missing antagonist. Where two answers fight for one scene, that is two pressures, and placing two pressures is `tens.tension_map`'s job rather than this card's.
**Best in:** formats: all | genres: all
**Avoid when:** **The thing in front of you is a named failure rather than a choice.** Twelve cards on this shelf carry *This is a named failure, not a recommendation*, and this map lists none of them; if your draft already does the thing, you are not selecting, you are repairing, and the repair is written on the failure card itself. Also **distrust axis 1 whenever your honest answer is its fourth value** — thirty-eight of the ninety-two reachable cards live there, so on a rhythm, medium or planning question this map has two questions left and is doing less than half the work it does on a scene with a danger in it. And **do not read axis 3 as a filter on genre**: its first value holds four cards, which is the shelf's own measured statement that almost nothing here survives under a minute, not an invitation to force something that does not. Finally, **the map is not the shelf, and two of its Axis 1 rows are contested.** `tens.polite_threat` carries a route to `tens.social_dread`, and a second reading of the same condition — *the power relationship is genuinely equal* — sends it to `tens.delay_by_digression` instead. `tens.picturable_consequence` carries a route to `tens.scale_dread`, and a second reading of *the threat's power depends on being unimaginable* sends it to `tens.refusing_to_name`. In both cases the two destinations sit under different values of Axis 1, so the answer moves depending on which reading is right. **Neither is settled here.** On those two cards, open both destinations before taking one.
**Prompt:** `[Selector — produces no prompt. It returns card ids. The chosen card carries the prompt.]`

---

**The axes**

**Axis 1 — What is the character up against, and could it be faced?**
Asked first, because it is the condition this shelf repeats most and the only one that decides whether the climax you are writing towards can exist at all. Fifteen of the ninety-three `Yields to:` lines turn on it, and four state it in almost the same words: *"where your climax has to be a confrontation. There is nothing to confront in an indifferent force"* (`tens.indifferent_force`), *"where your climax is a confrontation. You cannot confront what you have spent ninety minutes refusing to render"* (`tens.inferred_threat`), *"The audience came for a contest; give it a will"* (`tens.tension_without_villain`), *"where the audience must believe the protagonist can affect the outcome"* (`tens.scale_dread`). The rest sort the same way: *"where the asker has no power to act on the answer… an institution needs no leverage of its own"* (`tens.human_deadline`), *"No credible punisher; the cost is social"* (`tens.self_censorship`), *"where the pursuer is the slow, rule-bound kind"* (`tens.closing_pursuit`), *"Specify the system's gaps; bound the institution"* (`tens.total_surveillance`), *"With no mechanism by which discovery could occur the audience works it out in about four seconds"* (`tens.hiding_beat`), *"where the power relationship is genuinely equal"* (`tens.polite_threat`), *"The threat is a person; scale reach, not sight"* (`tens.reveal_clock`). The shelf even carries a card whose entire content is this question — `tens.embodied_vs_formless`, filed `only-one` in `PAIR-AUDIT.md` because nothing is an alternative to deciding.

**Axis 2 — Who is ahead, the audience or the characters?**
Nineteen conditions turn on this, and they are stated as structures rather than as feelings: *"where the unexpected ending* is *the point"* (`tens.bomb_under_table`), *"by default, on almost any scene whose content is talk"* (`tens.earned_surprise`, which names itself the exception and its converse the default), *"Announced doom and withheld outcome are opposite structures"* (`tens.known_outcome_dread`), *"where the threat is meant to be unknowable"* (`tens.rule_demonstration`), *"where the audience has to act on the information"* (`tens.refusing_to_name`), *"where the specificity is the thing you are deliberately withholding"* (`tens.specific_threat`), *"where the story's subject is the reality of the act itself"* (`tens.implication_over_depiction`), *"where the story needs the audience to know the truth of it"* (`tens.being_watched`), *"where you intend to explain it later"* (`tens.untrustworthy_environment`), *"where the story needs the audience to trust the protagonist's account for a later plot turn"* (`tens.unreliable_body`), *"with more than two candidates"* (`tens.suspect_ally`).

**Axis 3 — How much runway is there before the pressure has to already exist?**
Twelve conditions are about running time and nothing else, and eight of them route to the same card: *"under about a minute, where there is no room to hold the wait"* (`tens.dread_over_shock`), *"where you do not have the runway to establish the safety"* (`tens.safe_space_violation`), *"in vertical and short form, where dead air is a swipe"* (`tens.waiting_as_weapon`), *"in short form, where you cannot afford a minute of misdirection"* (`tens.delay_by_digression`), *"Short form; one near-miss is the whole chase"* (`tens.near_miss_economy`), *"Under five minutes there is no accumulated tension to discharge"* (`tens.trough_placement`), *"where there is no time for the audience to learn what leaving would cost"* (`tens.social_containment`), *"where a stop is a swipe"* (`tens.pursuit_that_pauses`). Its converse is stated once — *"Long-form, reader already committed; run the hum"* (`tens.first_five_seconds`) — and the boundary cases name their own numbers: *"Under ninety minutes, or an unbroken real-time clock"* (`tens.the_interval`), *"No room to teach the terrain's rule"* (`tens.terrain_pressure`). It is asked last because it is a gate rather than a sort: it removes almost everything or almost nothing.

**The default, and the one against it**

**The default is `tens.threat_with_rules` governing the danger and `tens.bomb_under_table` governing the scene — and it is measured, not asserted.** `tens.threat_with_rules` is the most-yielded-to danger card on the shelf: five cards send a reader to it, and all five send them for the same reason — *bound it so the audience can do the arithmetic.* `tens.closing_pursuit` (*"where the pursuer is the slow, rule-bound kind"*), `tens.adaptive_threat` (*"where the audience is keeping score against fixed rules"*), `tens.refusing_to_name` (*"where the audience has to act on the information"*), `tens.untrustworthy_environment` (*"commit to rules from the start"*) and `tens.total_surveillance` (*"Specify the system's gaps; bound the institution"*). Nothing else about a danger is named more than three times. On the scene side `tens.bomb_under_table` takes three inbound routes and, uniquely on this shelf, **declares itself the default in its own pair field**: *"this card is the default only because you almost always get more minutes out of telling the audience."* The shelf, asked ninety-three times where to fall back to, falls back to a bounded threat the audience has already been told about.

**One measured caveat, because it changes what the word default means here.** The single most-yielded-to card on the whole shelf is neither of those — it is `tens.micro_form_tension`, with eight inbound routes, more than threat and scene combined. But every one of the eight fires on the same condition, *short form*, and `tens.micro_form_tension` is one of only four cards under Axis 3's first value. **The shelf's most-named card is a format escape hatch, not a fallback**, and reading in-degree without reading the conditions would have made it the default and made this selector wrong.

**The one against it is `tens.self_censorship`.** Nothing on the shelf routes to it; it is named by no `Yields to:` anywhere in the family; and it is the only card here whose content is a non-event — *"the thing the character decides in advance not to do. Nothing happens, deliberately, and that has to be staged as an event."* Every other card on this shelf puts a wrongness into the frame and then manages how much of it the audience gets. This one puts nothing into the frame and makes the absence legible, which is the opposite move and the harder one. Its stated cost is a qualification rather than a weakness — it needs a credible punisher, and without one the character reads as timid instead of pressured — so it is a card you earn the right to use rather than one you fall back on. **Its near cousin against the grain is `tens.ritual_that_must_continue`**, likewise never yielded to, and the shelf's only card where the pressure comes from a form being observed *correctly*: everything proceeds exactly as it should, and that is the trap. Between them they are the two places on this shelf where the tension is made of nothing going wrong.

**And the shape of that list is the finding, not its length.**

**First: the pair graph never crosses a medium.** Nine cards on this shelf exist because a delivery channel changes what tension can be — `tens.audio_no_offscreen`, `tens.room_tone_silence`, `tens.prose_no_soundtrack`, `tens.reader_owns_the_clock`, `tens.page_turn`, `tens.stage_blackout`, `tens.the_interval`, `tens.interactive_tension`, `tens.subtitle_preempt`. **Seven of the nine are on the list above**, and the two that are not receive exactly one inbound route each, both from inside their own medium: `tens.room_tone_silence` → `tens.audio_no_offscreen` (audio to audio) and `tens.the_interval` → `tens.stage_blackout` (theatre to theatre). Not one route in the family crosses from film into prose, from prose into audio, or from anything into a game. The readers who wrote these ninety-three fields were each holding one medium, and **a medium is not an alternative to a device — it is the room the device is standing in**, which is a thing the pair field has no grammar for. That is why these cards route outward, to `rhythm.`, `inter.` and `expo.`, or nowhere at all.

**Second, and this one names a missing card: nothing on this shelf points at the audience's remaining capacity.** Four cards treat that capacity as the real resource — `tens.near_miss_economy` (*"a currency with a small balance… the account empties faster than writers expect"*), `tens.trough_placement`, `tens.release_valve`, and the named failure `tens.exhausting_draft` (*"pressure applied continuously until the reader withdraws in self-defence"*). **All four are unreachable through the pair graph**: three are on the list above, and the fourth is a failure nothing routes to. `tens.near_miss_economy` is the only card in a hundred and four carrying an explicit balance-and-spend model, and it applies that model to exactly one device. **The card this shelf wants is the one that says every device on it draws on the same account** — that a near-miss, a false scare, a shrinking room and a held silence all debit one running total, and that `tens.exhausting_draft` is the overdraft notice arriving after the fact, with no meter anywhere on the shelf to read beforehand.

**Third, a structural note that is his to settle rather than mine.** Three cards — `tens.instruction_under_stress`, `tens.warning_notice` and the named failure `tens.warning_fatigue` — form a closed island: `tens.warning_fatigue` → `tens.warning_notice` → `tens.instruction_under_stress` → off-shelf, and **nothing in the other hundred and one cards routes into the island and nothing in the island routes back out.** They are not story tension at all; they are functional copy written for a reader whose comprehension has collapsed. They are mapped here because `SHELVES.md` puts them on this shelf, and they sit together under Axis 1's second value and Axis 3's first. If `tens.` is ever split, that is where the seam runs.

`tens.pressure_before_device`
